questions.title: Too many meetings, too few decisions
questions.prompt: Product managers in your 80-person product organisation say they spend half their week in reviews and status meetings, yet decisions still take weeks. Redesign the operating cadence.
hints: What information could move to written updates?
Who must be in which decision?
followups: A senior executive loves their weekly review. What do you do?
How do you know the new cadence works?
What do you do with decisions that do not fit any forum?
criteria: Inventories forums and classifies them (decide, inform, align).
Replaces information meetings with written updates.
Maps decisions to forums with clear owners and inputs.
Pilots changes and measures time spent and decision speed.
Handles senior stakeholders respectfully.
outline: Inventory every recurring forum: purpose, attendees, hours, decisions made.
Remove or replace inform-only meetings with written updates.
Map decision types to forums: planning, product reviews, launch go/no-go.
Standard inputs (one-pager template) shared in advance.
Pilot for a quarter; measure PM hours in meetings and decision lead time.
Executive reviews: keep, but change format to decisions.
questions.reference:
I would start with an inventory: every recurring meeting, its purpose, attendees, hours consumed and decisions actually made in the last month. Usually many are status updates that inform but do not decide.

Inform-only meetings become written updates in a standard format. Decisions are mapped to a few forums — quarterly planning, a weekly product review for decisions that need leadership, launch go/no-go — each with a clear owner, required inputs shared in advance, and a decision log.

I would pilot the new cadence for a quarter with a few teams and measure hours PMs spend in meetings and time from a decision being needed to being made. For an executive who loves their weekly review, I would keep it but change the format: pre-reads and decisions only. Decisions that do not fit any forum go to the product lead with a short written proposal.
pitfalls: Adding a new meeting to fix meetings.

questions.title: The feedback graveyard
questions.prompt: Customer feedback arrives through support tickets, sales notes, research interviews and app reviews, but PMs say they never see it in a usable form. Build the insights system.
hints: How do you make feedback from different sources comparable?
How do you weight feedback by customer value?
How do customers learn that their feedback mattered?
followups: Sales keeps logging 'must-have' requests for single customers. How do you handle that?
Should you use AI to tag feedback? What are the risks?
How do you know PMs use it?
criteria: Centralises sources with consistent tagging.
Links feedback to customers and their value.
Produces regular, digestible theme reports for product reviews.
Closes the loop with customers.
Measures use by PMs.
outline: Sources into one repository with links to originals.
Taxonomy: product area, problem theme, severity; customer segment and revenue.
Tagging: assisted, with human checks.
Output: monthly themes per area into product reviews; searchable for PMs.
Close the loop: notify customers when themes ship.
Measure: PMs citing insights in specs; time to find evidence.
questions.reference:
I would bring all sources into one repository, each item linked to its original and to the customer and segment it came from. A shared taxonomy — product area, problem theme, severity — makes support tickets and interview notes comparable. Tagging can be assisted by a model to save time, but with human review of a sample, because mis-tagging silently distorts priorities.

Weighting matters: a theme raised by many small customers and one raised by a single large one are both important in different ways, so reports show frequency and the revenue of customers affected. Sales ‘must-haves’ are logged like everything else, with the customer and deal named, so their weight is visible rather than loud.

Output: a monthly theme report per product area feeding product reviews, plus search for PMs writing specs. When a theme ships, customers who raised it hear about it. Success: PMs cite customer evidence in specs and find it in minutes rather than days.

questions.title: Launches that surprise support
questions.prompt: Three recent launches surprised the support team: customers asked about features support had never heard of. Design a launch process that prevents this without slowing teams down.
hints: Do all launches need the same process?
Who must be ready, and by when?
followups: Teams say the checklist is too long. What do you cut?
How do you handle small, frequent changes?
How do you know the process works?
criteria: Tiers launches by customer impact.
Defines readiness requirements per tier (support, docs, sales, legal).
Single launch calendar visible to all.
Clear go/no-go owner.
Measures surprises and launch quality.
outline: Tiers: major (marketing, sales), standard (customer-visible), minor (internal or tiny).
Per tier: readiness checklist and lead time.
Calendar: one shared place; support subscribes.
Go/no-go: PM owns, with support and docs sign-off for tiers 1–2.
Small changes: weekly release notes to support.
Measure: support tickets about unknown features; post-launch reviews.
questions.reference:
I would tier launches by customer impact. Major launches (announced, priced) need sales enablement, support training, documentation and marketing, with a few weeks’ lead time. Standard customer-visible changes need support notes and documentation a week before. Minor changes go into weekly release notes. Most launches are small, so most teams see little extra process.

Every customer-facing launch goes on one shared calendar that support, sales and success can see. For the top two tiers, go/no-go is owned by the PM with sign-off from support and documentation — they can block if they are not ready.

To keep it light, the checklist per tier is short and reviewed each quarter to remove items that never catch problems. Success: support tickets about features support did not know about drop to near zero, and teams report the process as quick in a short survey.
pitfalls: One heavy process for every change.

questions.title: Four roadmap tools
questions.prompt: Teams in your product organisation keep roadmaps in four different tools, so leadership cannot see a single picture. Fix it.
hints: What do leaders need to see, and how often?
What do teams need from their tools day to day?
Is the problem the tools or the lack of a shared format?
followups: One team refuses to move from its tool. Now what?
How do you keep the roadmap current?
Would you buy a new tool?
criteria: Separates leadership's needs from teams' daily needs.
Prefers a shared format and source of truth over forcing one tool.
Integrates or migrates with clear reasons.
Keeps data current through ownership and cadence.
Avoids buying a tool for a process problem.
outline: Needs: leaders want outcomes, status, dates and dependencies; teams want task-level flexibility.
Define a standard roadmap item format (outcome, status, confidence, dates).
Source of truth: one system for roadmap items; team tools for execution, linked.
Migration: teams with no strong need move first; integrations for the rest.
Currency: monthly review; owners update before planning forums.
questions.reference:
First, separate needs. Leaders need a consistent view of outcomes, status, confidence, timing and dependencies. Teams need flexible tools for daily work. Forcing everyone into one execution tool usually fails; agreeing a shared roadmap format and one source of truth for roadmap items usually works.

I would define the roadmap item — outcome, owner, status, confidence, target quarter, dependencies — and pick the system most teams already use as the source of truth for those items, linked to whatever teams use for tasks. Teams without strong needs move first; teams with special needs get an integration.

The roadmap stays current because owners update it before each monthly planning forum, where it is the only document used. I would buy a new tool only if no existing one can hold the shared format — the problem is usually process, not software.

questions.title: Is the product organisation healthy?
questions.prompt: The Chief Product Officer asks you for a quarterly 'health of the product organisation' report. What do you measure, and how do you avoid it becoming a tool for ranking PMs?
hints: Health of what: delivery, outcomes, quality, people?
Which measures are about the system rather than individuals?
What will the CPO do with the report?
followups: The CPO asks for a per-PM breakdown. How do you respond?
Which measure is most likely to be gamed?
How do you show trends honestly?
criteria: Covers flow, outcomes, quality and people.
Measures at team or organisation level.
Uses trends and context, not single numbers.
Explicitly avoids individual ranking; explains why.
Links measures to actions.
outline: Flow: idea-to-launch lead time; share of planned work delivered.
Outcomes: share of goals met; experiments with clear results.
Quality: incidents, rollbacks, customer-reported defects.
People: engagement survey, attrition, PM-to-engineer ratios.
Format: trends by area with commentary; actions.
Avoid ranking: system measures; individuals are a management conversation.
questions.reference:
I would cover four areas, measured at team or organisation level. Flow: time from approved idea to launch, and the share of planned work delivered. Outcomes: share of quarterly goals met, and experiments that produced a clear decision. Quality: incidents and rollbacks caused by launches, customer-reported defects. People: engagement survey results, attrition and staffing ratios.

The report shows trends over several quarters with commentary — why a measure moved and what we are doing — because single numbers invite wrong conclusions.

If the CPO asks for a per-PM breakdown, I would explain that these measures depend on teams, products and dependencies, so per-person numbers would mislead and would quickly be gamed. Individual performance belongs in management conversations with richer context. The report’s purpose is to improve the system: each issue it shows gets an action and an owner.

questions.title: A process you removed
questions.prompt: Tell me about a process you introduced or removed that changed how a team worked.
hints: How did you get people to change?
How did you know it worked?
criteria: Clear problem.
Involved the people affected.
Measured the result.
Adjusted based on feedback.
Lasting change.
outline: Problem.
Change.
How you involved people.
Result and measure.
Adjustments.
Lesson.
questions.reference: A strong answer (a model of structure, not a script): “Our weekly roadmap review had grown to 25 people and rarely decided anything. I proposed replacing it with written updates and a 30-minute decision meeting with six people. I tested it with two product areas for a month, measured meeting hours and the time to decisions, and shared the results. Both improved, so the rest of the organisation adopted it. Six months later we still use it, with one change suggested by PMs: a monthly open session for questions.”
